prompt: Every pattern in the 1994 book ends with its consequences. What is that part for?

choices.text: It lists the programs that already use the pattern, as proof that it works
choices.why: The book gives known uses elsewhere; the consequences are about costs.

choices.text: Saying what the pattern costs
choices.why: Right. Every pattern adds indirection, and this part says when that pays.

choices.text: Giving the C++ code to copy into your program
choices.why: A pattern is a shape, not code to copy; the code differs in every program.

prompt: The book's introduction says: program to an interface, and favour object ___ over class inheritance.
The library starts lending board games. With the factory in factory.py, what has to change besides the new class?

choices.text: Every function that reads rows, to add a branch for games
choices.why: That is the scattered if the factory exists to remove.

choices.text: One entry in KINDS
choices.why: Right. The string-to-class decision lives in one dictionary.

choices.text: Loan.for_item, so that it knows how long a game is lent for
choices.why: for_item reads loan_days from the item, whatever its class.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because the factory discovers new classes on its own
choices.why: It discovers nothing; an unknown kind is refused by name, as vinyl was.

prompt: Why does QueryBuilder check the column in order_by rather than leaving it to build?

choices.text: A step refuses bad input as it arrives, before any SQL
choices.why: Right. That validation is one of the reasons a builder earns its place.

choices.text: build is unable to raise exceptions in Python
choices.why: Any method can raise; checking early is a choice about where errors show up.

choices.text: SQLite refuses ORDER BY on a column it was not told about first
choices.why: The column is pasted into the text, so only the builder's list stands between a caller and arbitrary SQL there.

prompt: A Python dataclass has nine fields, seven of them optional with sensible defaults, all set in one place. A colleague proposes a builder. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: A builder, since Java code uses one in the same situation
choices.why: Java uses builders because it lacks keyword arguments; Python has them.

choices.text: A factory dictionary keyed by the combination of fields
choices.why: A factory chooses a class; here there is one class and many optional values.

choices.text: Named parameters with fallback values, which it already has
choices.why: Right. A builder pays when steps validate or the object is assembled in several places.

choices.text: A singleton holding the default values shared by every instance of the class
choices.why: Defaults belong to the fields; a global object would add shared state and nothing else.

prompt: In singleton.py, desk_b printed a fine of 75 although it never set one. Why?

choices.text: Settings reads the fine from a file that desk_a wrote
choices.why: Nothing touches a file; the value lives on the one shared instance.

choices.text: desk_a changed the one Settings object, which is the same object desk_b got
choices.why: Right. Global access means a change anywhere is seen everywhere, by code that never asked.

choices.text: Python caches function results, so desk_b repeated desk_a's answer
choices.why: Python caches nothing here unless asked; the shared object is the cause.

prompt: Why is an object created at module level in Python already a singleton?

choices.text: Python forbids creating a second instance of any class defined in a module
choices.why: You can create as many Catalogue objects as you like; only shared is created once.

choices.text: Module-level names are copied into every importing file
choices.why: If they were copies, shared is catalogue.shared would be False; it printed True.

choices.text: A module runs once and is cached, so every import gets the same object
choices.why: Right. Two imports under two names printed True.

prompt: The library needs exactly one catalogue in memory, and its tests keep interfering with each other. Which design does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Keep the singleton and add a reset() method called by every test
choices.why: That is a method that exists only to undo the pattern, and a forgotten call brings the leak back.

choices.text: Create one in the composition root and pass it in
choices.why: Right. Still exactly one, without access from everywhere, and each test can hand in a fresh one.

choices.text: Make the singleton thread-safe with a lock around __new__
choices.why: A lock fixes double creation under threads; the tests still share one instance.

prompt: The national catalogue renames its field ttl to title. With OpenShelfCatalogue in place, what changes?

choices.text: Every function that shows a book, wherever it reads the field
choices.why: Those functions read Book.title; they never saw ttl.

choices.text: Book, which gains a ttl field so both names work
choices.why: Our model does not follow theirs; that is the point of the border.

choices.text: One line in the adapter's find method
choices.why: Right. The adapter is where the foreign model stops.

choices.text: LendingDesk, because the facade sits in front of the catalogue
choices.why: The facade asks a Catalogue for a Book and is untouched by the service's format.

prompt: What does LendingDesk do that makes it a facade rather than an adapter?

choices.text: It gives several objects one simpler door
choices.why: Right. Catalogue, reservations, ledger and printer, behind one lend.

choices.text: It translates the service's record format into a Book
choices.why: That is what OpenShelfCatalogue does, the adapter it is handed.

choices.text: It hides the Ledger so that no other code may ever read the loans
choices.why: A facade adds a door; the monthly report can still use Ledger directly.

prompt: Your code expects a Notifier with send(member, text). A new SMS company's library offers dispatch(phone_number, body, sender_id). What do you write?

choices.text: A facade over the SMS library and the e-mail library together
choices.why: Nothing here asks for one door to several things; one interface needs to look like another.

choices.text: An adapter, translating each call into the other
choices.why: Right. It does what you need and speaks the wrong language, which is the adapter's question.

choices.text: A proxy, because the SMS company is another process
choices.why: A proxy keeps the same interface; here the interfaces differ.

choices.text: Rename send to dispatch everywhere in your code
choices.why: That lets a vendor's names into your whole program, and the next vendor renames them again.

prompt: student = Capped(GraceDays(DailyFine(50), days=2), cap=1000). What does student.fine(5) return, in cents?
hint: Follow the call inwards, then the value back out.

prompt: GraceDays and CachingCatalogue are built the same way. What makes one a decorator and the other a proxy?

choices.text: A decorator must change the interface, and a proxy must keep it
choices.why: Both keep the interface; that is what lets them stand in for the wrapped object.

choices.text: The intent: one adds behaviour, the other controls access
choices.why: Right. The structure is identical, and the name tells the reader which job it does.

choices.text: A proxy has to talk to another process over the network
choices.why: That is one kind, the remote proxy; CachingCatalogue is in the same process.

prompt: An ORM returns a loan whose member is loaded from the database only when code first touches loan.member. Which kind of proxy is that?

choices.text: A protection proxy, since it decides who may read the member
choices.why: Nothing is checked; everybody gets the member, just later.

choices.text: A decorator, since it adds loading to the member
choices.why: Loading is access, not added behaviour the caller chose; the caller does not even know it is there.

choices.text: A virtual proxy, delaying the load until it is needed
choices.why: Right. It delays creating something expensive until it is used.

choices.text: A remote proxy, because the database runs in another process
choices.why: The defining trait here is the delay, not where the data lives.

prompt: The committee wants a third rule: members who have waited longest on any list go first. What changes in strategy.py?

choices.text: A new class with an order method, handed to WaitingList
choices.why: Right. WaitingList delegates the decision and stays as it is.

choices.text: An if inside WaitingList.queue that checks which rule is active
choices.why: That puts the decision back in the context, which is what the strategy removed.

choices.text: A subclass of WaitingList for each rule the committee tries
choices.why: Then the rule could not change while the list lives, as ordering did in the run.

prompt: In observer.py, ReservationAlert raises an exception. What happens to ReturnCount, subscribed after it?

choices.text: It is told anyway, because each listener runs in its own thread
choices.why: give_back calls listeners one after another in the same thread.

choices.text: It is never told: the exception stops the loop
choices.why: Right. Production code catches per listener, and then has to decide what a failed listener means.

choices.text: ReturnsDesk unsubscribes the failing listener and carries on with the next
choices.why: Nothing in give_back catches anything; that would have to be written.

choices.text: Python retries the alert until it succeeds, then tells the count
choices.why: Python retries nothing on its own.

prompt: Reading ReturnsDesk.give_back, a new developer cannot tell that returns trigger reservation alerts. Is that a defect of this code?

choices.text: Yes: the alert belongs inside give_back, where everybody can see it
choices.why: Then the desk would grow a line for every reaction, which is what observer avoids.

choices.text: It is the known price of observer: the desk stops knowing what follows a return
choices.why: Right. Decoupling the subject is the point and also the cost; the answer lives with whoever subscribed.

choices.text: Yes: the listeners should be passed to give_back on every call
choices.why: Every caller would then have to know every reaction, which moves the coupling rather than removing it.

prompt: Put the states of the copy in state.py in the order the run went through them.
items: on loan to Bia, Caio waiting
trap: Duda's requests changed nothing: a refusal leaves the state where it was.

prompt: Why does Return set self.member inside execute rather than take it in its constructor?

choices.text: Commands are not allowed to take arguments in their constructors, by the pattern's rules
choices.why: Lend takes three; Return takes two.

choices.text: Who had the book is known only once it runs; undo needs it
choices.why: Right. A command keeps whatever it needs to reverse itself.

choices.text: So that the desk can print the member in its history
choices.why: __str__ for Return prints only the title.

prompt: WaitingList holds an Ordering and Copy holds a state, both behind an interface. What tells the two patterns apart?

choices.text: State has three methods, while a strategy has exactly one method by definition
choices.why: A strategy may have several methods; the count is not the difference.

choices.text: A strategy may be a function, while a state is a class
choices.why: A dictionary of transitions or a match can stand in for state classes; the lesson says so.

choices.text: Who replaces the object: a caller swaps a strategy, a state replaces itself
choices.why: Right. Copy never has its state set from outside; WaitingList never changes its own ordering.

prompt: In template.py, which part of a report can a subclass not change?

choices.text: The footer
choices.why: OverdueReport overrides it.

choices.text: How each row is formatted, which only the base class decides
choices.why: format_row is a hook with a default; any subclass may override it.

choices.text: The order in which render calls the steps, fixed by the base class
choices.why: Right. The base class owns the outline and calls the subclass's steps.

prompt: Shelf.__iter__ contains a yield. What does that give the method?

choices.text: It makes the shelf return a list of every book
choices.why: Nothing is collected into a list; one pair is produced per request.

choices.text: Calling it now returns an iterator object, with __next__ already written for you
choices.why: Right. A generator is the GoF iterator that Python writes for you, what MarkWalker spells out.

choices.text: It runs the loop on another thread, so the shelf stays responsive
choices.why: A generator runs in the caller's thread, a step at a time.

choices.text: It sorts the shelf marks, which a plain return would not
choices.why: The sorting is done by MarkWalker; yield only hands out each pair.

prompt: What did Peter Norvig's 1996 talk find about the 23 patterns in Lisp and Dylan?

choices.text: That every one of them was wrong and should be abandoned
choices.why: He found many simpler or invisible there, not wrong; the ideas survive.

choices.text: That 16 were simpler or invisible there
choices.why: Right. First-class functions, classes as objects and macros did their work.

choices.text: That those languages needed more patterns than C++, being dynamic
choices.why: The finding went the other way: features made patterns shrink.

prompt: Which of these patterns shrink to a language feature in Python? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Strategy, as a function passed to sorted
choices.why: Right. key= has been the strategy pattern all along.

choices.text: Iterator, as a generator with yield
choices.why: Right. yield writes the __next__ for you.

choices.text: Facade, as a built-in keyword
choices.why: Facade is about dividing responsibilities, and stays a class in every language.

choices.text: Command with undo, as partial saved in a list
choices.why: Right. vanish.py undid a loan with one saved function.

prompt: Match each problem at the library to the pattern that answers it.

pairs.left: The rule for who gets a reserved book changes every term
The desk must undo its last actions
A copy must refuse a loan while it is held for somebody
A slow outside catalogue is asked the same question all day

prompt: A payment library returns its own Charge objects, and three screens need to start a loan with a fine paid first. Which pair of patterns fits?

choices.text: Two singletons, one for payments and one for loans
choices.why: One instance each solves nothing here, and adds global state.

choices.text: An adapter for the payment library and a facade for the three screens
choices.why: Right. The adapter stops their model at the border; the facade gives the screens one door.

choices.text: Observer and decorator
choices.why: Nothing needs announcing and nothing needs layering; the problems are a foreign model and a multi-step flow.

choices.text: A builder for the Charge objects and an iterator over the screens
choices.why: Charges come built by the library; what is missing is translation and coordination.

prompt: A Go colleague says their service uses no strategy pattern, yet it sorts with sort.Slice(loans, func(i, j int) bool {...}). What is the fairest reply?

choices.text: The function passed in is a strategy; Go simply needs no class to hold it
choices.why: Right. The idea survives the language: a decision separated from the code that uses it.

choices.text: She is right, because Go has no classes and so cannot have patterns
choices.why: Patterns are shapes of a design, not classes; Go code is full of them.

choices.text: It is a template method, since sort.Slice fixes the outline
choices.why: Template method fills steps by subclassing; here the step is passed in, which is strategy.
